name: Negativity Bias
description: Negative information, outcomes, and experiences weigh more heavily than equally positive ones. One bad moment can dominate how users remember and judge an otherwise good experience.
design_relevance_note: Explains why error states, broken promises, hostile copy, dark-pattern suspicion, or one failed payment/login event can overpower many smoothly designed moments.
prevalence_note: Frequently invoked in service recovery, trust, content, and error-state design, but less often foregrounded as a named first-tier UX law than Fitts's, Hick's, or Jakob's Law.

findings.description: Across a wide range of domains — everyday events, major life events, close relationships, social networks, interpersonal interactions, self-perception, impression formation, and learning — negative information and events consistently exert a stronger psychological effect than equivalent positive ones. The asymmetry persists after controlling for alternative explanations like salience or diagnosticity, and the review found 'hardly any exceptions' to the pattern across the entire literature surveyed.

applications.title: COVID-19 dashboards displaying cumulative case counts distorting perceived crisis severity
applications.description: Early COVID-19 dashboards displayed cumulative (ever-growing, never-decreasing) case counts rather than current active cases or trends -- a presentation choice that, given negativity bias, can distort a viewer's perception of whether a situation is actually improving or worsening at any given moment.
applications.ethical_note: This isn't attributed to one specific named dashboard, unlike other entries in this batch -- it's a general critique of a widely-used convention across real COVID-19 dashboards. Graded unclear rather than assigning a persuasion-intent verdict, since the cumulative-count convention was very plausibly a data-reporting norm rather than a deliberate emotional-framing decision, and the source itself doesn't allege intent either way.

applications.title: Four Seasons' curt error message making a bad situation feel worse
applications.description: A Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts error message was described as stilted and impolite, compounding a user's already-negative moment (something going wrong) with an unsympathetic tone rather than a considerate one.
applications.ethical_note: A tone/microcopy quality issue with no persuasion or manipulation angle -- an unsympathetic error message harms the user's experience, but there's no deceptive or exploitative intent involved.

applications.title: MailChimp's friendly, empathetic tone counteracting negative moments
applications.description: MailChimp is presented as a positive example of using a friendly, empathetic tone in its interface copy and interactions, intended to counteract negativity bias by making even routine or mildly frustrating moments feel less unpleasant.
applications.ethical_note: A genuine tone-of-voice choice with no manipulative angle -- being kind in copy costs the company nothing deceptive and directly benefits the user's experience.
